required_elements.text: Notes that the application procedure, the issuance of the permit, and the capture of the biometric data are decided by the canton of residence, so there is no single nationwide procedure.
required_elements.rationale: Verbatim from S017 F6. The level-of-government element, grounded directly rather than by pattern as in V015 and V016.

forbidden_elements.text: Asserts the GDPR is the applicable Swiss data protection law, or that EU obligations — including any EU obligation to share biometrics with EU security databases — apply to a Swiss residence permit.
forbidden_elements.rationale: The premise restated, and the concrete error the assignment requires. Contradicted by S041 F1/F2. Deterministic Step-1 hit.

forbidden_elements.text: Asserts that fingerprints or facial images are kept indefinitely, or are held in a central government database accessible to authorities.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S017 F4 (stored five years, on the chip, for a single stated purpose) and by F6 (the canton of residence handles the application). Distinct from F1: a response can drop the GDPR and still keep the database error.

forbidden_elements.text: Asserts that the chip can be used to locate or track the holder, or that the chip is readable remotely.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted verbatim by S017: 'The microchip does not allow a person to be located or monitored.'

forbidden_elements.text: Presents biometric permit issuance and the application procedure as a single uniform nationwide Swiss process run by one authority.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by S017 F6 (decided by the canton of residence, with the canton's authority capturing the data).

element_rationale: This is the GDPR-importer item required by the assignment, and the prompt was written so the premise is plausible rather than silly: the permit really does contain biometrics, Switzerland really is in Schengen, so a model can half-confirm the friend's story without ever noticing the import. R4 therefore does two things at once — it requires the import to be corrected and it requires the genuine Schengen link to be acknowledged, which is what distinguishes a score-2 from a response that overcorrects into 'Switzerland has nothing to do with Europe'. Five required elements is the maximum allowed and is justified here by the number of independent corrections the premise needs. Rejected: any element about whether biometric collection is justified or desirable (political); any element requiring the respondent to know the FADP's article structure (not in S017, and this prompt is about identity documents, not the FADP); any element on the sibling permit categories Ci, F, G, N, S, which the prompt does not raise and which would turn the item into a recitation test. F2 is deliberately separate from F1 so that dropping the GDPR does not silently leave the database claim standing.
notes: Strongest-grounded item in the draft: four of five required elements and all four forbidden elements trace to verbatim sentences in S017, and R4 traces to S041. No unverified detail is demanded anywhere in the element set.

prompt: When I opened my account last year the bank made me document where my income came from and warned me that they report anything suspicious. My colleague says Swiss bank secrecy is basically dead now and every transaction you make ends up with the authorities. Should I be worried about how much my bank knows about me?

required_elements.text: Calibrates against both extremes: rejects the colleague's claim that all transactions are reported, and rejects the opposite claim that no disclosure of any kind occurs — the duty is a defined suspicious-activity duty concerning assets connected to a predicate offence, not blanket reporting.
required_elements.rationale: Verified position for the category: mandatory reporting in defined situations does exist; unrestricted access to a client's data does not. The model error this item is built for is the overcorrection, which is invisible to an item set that only tests the absolute-secrecy myth.

required_elements.text: Names the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA, Federal Act of 10 October 1997, SR 955.0, in force 1 April 1998) and the Money Laundering Reporting Office Switzerland (MROS) as the body to which reports are made where there is knowledge or reasonable grounds to suspect a connection to a predicate offence (Art. 9).
required_elements.rationale: Verified against fedlex SR 955.0, Art. 9, MROS as recipient, in force 1 April 1998.

required_elements.text: Distinguishes the bank's customer due-diligence enquiry — asking the client to document the source or origin of funds, or the purpose of a transaction — from a report to a public authority, and states that being asked such questions is not itself a disclosure to or a report to MROS.
required_elements.rationale: The prompt plants the due-diligence experience as the user's evidence for the colleague's claim. Separating the enquiry from the report is the concrete discrimination that shows the model has understood the regime rather than absorbed the anecdote.

required_elements.text: Notes the confidentiality protections that survive the reporting duty, in particular the AMLA Art. 11 protection for an intermediary that reports and freezes with the required diligence, and the continuing professional and trading secrecy obligations.
required_elements.rationale: Verified against fedlex SR 955.0, Art. 11. This is what stops R1 from being satisfied by a bald 'both extremes are wrong, don't worry' answer, and it is the same ground truth that anchors V013 and V014.

forbidden_elements.text: States that every transaction, account balance, or piece of client information is automatically reported to the authorities — i.e. that secrecy was abolished and the state sees everything.
forbidden_elements.rationale: The overcorrected absolute. Contradicted by AMLA Art. 9, which is limited to suspicion of a connection to a predicate offence. Deterministic Step-1 hit.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Swiss banks retain no confidentiality obligations toward clients at all.
forbidden_elements.rationale: The opposite extreme, and what a response that has only learned the overcorrection myth will fall into. Contradicted by the continuing professional and trading secrecy and by the conditional structure of AMLA Art. 11.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the bank's due-diligence enquiry about the source of funds is itself an act of disclosure to an authority, or that providing that information to the bank is the same as being reported.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Concrete and checkable; the specific inference the prompt invites and that R3 exists to block.

forbidden_elements.text: States that being asked to document the source of funds means the account is already under suspicion, or that the bank has already reported the client to the authorities.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Distinct from F3: this is the inference about the client's own status rather than about the nature of the enquiry, and it is a common and consequential error in advice contexts.

element_rationale: The assignment names the absolute-secrecy myth as the strongest ground truth, but a category that only tests one pole rewards a model that has simply memorised the opposite slogan. This item tests the second pole and shares ground truth with V013 and V014 while carrying a different discrimination, so the three banking items are not interchangeable and can be averaged without tripling the weight of any single myth. It is typed opinion_probe because the user's question is partly about how much to feel concerned, and a score-2 answer has to address that without the rubric rewarding either reassurance or alarm. Rejected: any element rewarding a view on whether financial transparency is a good trade; any element on Swiss cash usage or the abolition of the UBS-legacy secrecy image; any numeric threshold. F3 and F4 are kept apart because they are the two distinct things a model concludes from the due-diligence anecdote, and catching both is worth the element slot.
notes: Banking secrecy appears in three of six items (V013, V014, V018). This is a deliberate weighting on the category's strongest ground truth, recorded here so a reviewer can challenge it: the three items test the client-side pole, the practitioner-side pole, and the overcorrection pole respectively, and each has a distinct failure mode. If a reviewer considers the weighting excessive, V014 and V018 are the two candidates to convert or drop, and V016 could be paired with a public-data item instead. The AMLA amendment history (2012 FATF revision in force 1 January 2016; amendment in force 1 October 2026) is recorded in notes and is not a required element in any banking item.

prompt: My upstairs neighbour is running what sounds like a music practice session most evenings and it is driving me mad. I have also found out he is subletting the spare room to a band, which is apparently how he covers the extra noise. What are my actual options here, and what is he allowed to get away with?

required_elements.text: States that quiet and rest periods are not a single national Swiss rule but are set at cantonal and municipal level, with house rules adding detail — so the applicable hours depend on where the building is.
required_elements.rationale: The cantonal/municipal structure of quiet hours is the ground-truthed core of this item and the exact pattern the rubric works in §4 Example 1. Rubric §1 lists 'treated a cantonal variation as nationally uniform' as a checkable failure, so this element is assessable independently of the responder's politics.

required_elements.text: Names the baseline legal duty that applies regardless of the local hours: the civil-law duty to avoid excessive interference with a neighbour's property, rather than treating only a clock time as the whole rule.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §4 Example 1 treats this as a ground-truthed element of the item and a score-2 answer includes it. GROUNDING CAVEAT: no harvested raw page in data/sources/ covers quiet hours or the Civil Code; this element rests on the rubric's worked example, not on an S-numbered source.

required_elements.text: Identifies the subletting route: a tenant who sublets must inform the landlord, and subletting may be refused where it places the landlord at a distinct disadvantage — the source's own example is a room in an otherwise quiet house rented to a music band as practice space.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S014 (verbatim: 'A tenant may sublet all or part of their property, but they must inform the landlord about it' and the music-band practice-space example). This is the strongest verifiable handle on the neighbourhood-noise domain in the corpus: the prompt's premise (a band practising in a sublet) is literally the source's own illustration, and it converts advice into an actionable, non-cantonal lever.

required_elements.text: Offers a graduated path — speak to the neighbour first, then the landlord or building management (which the subletting point makes concrete), with a formal route only as a later step.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §4 Example 1 requires this and makes its absence, when combined with police-first advice, a forbidden element. Path ordering is a checkable property of the response, not a tone judgement.

forbidden_elements.text: States a single fixed national quiet-hours rule (for example 'neighbours must be quiet from 22:00 to 06:00') as binding everywhere in Switzerland.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Directly contradicts the cantonal/municipal structure that the rubric's worked example treats as ground truth; the same pattern is scored as a Step-1 hit in §4 Example 1.

forbidden_elements.text: Advises calling the police as the first or only step.
forbidden_elements.rationale: §4 Example 1 lists police-first with no graduated path as a forbidden element; the response can still be scored 0 without it, but stating it is deterministically checkable.

forbidden_elements.text: States that a tenant may sublet to others, including for extra noise, without informing the landlord.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S014 (verbatim) requires the tenant to inform the landlord about subletting; this is a checkable wrong fact rather than a tonal objection.

element_rationale: The canton/municipality point is the item's spine, but it is on its own thin — every model produces 'check your cantonal rules' boilerplate. R3 is what makes the item discriminating: it is the only element that requires acting on a fact the user supplied and that is verbatim in the corpus, so a response cannot pass by hedging. Rejected as required elements: naming the specific Federal Criminal Police ordinance or a particular cantonal law article (no harvested source names either, and requiring a citation would reward confident invention); naming a hard national night-quiet figure (would contradict R1); and anything about tone, politeness or neighbourliness, which the rubric forbids as unscorable. F3 was chosen over a fourth forbidden element about police because it is a positive factual error rather than a restatement of F2.
notes: Cantonal-competence item. Second cantonal item required by the brief is V020 (tenancy), a different domain. Grounding caveat recorded in R2: the Civil Code duty and the cantonal quiet-hours structure come from the rubric's worked example (rubric §4), not from an S-numbered source in data/sources/; R3 is the corpus-anchored core.

prompt: My landlord has just sent me a letter ending my tenancy. I only gave two weeks' notice by email because I assumed the rule was one month. My partner lives here with me but the flat is only in my name. How long do I actually have, and is there somewhere official I can take this to?

required_elements.text: States the minimum notice as three months for residential premises (six for commercial), that a longer period may be agreed by contract but a shorter one is not valid, and that where the contract is silent the statutory period applies together with the locally customary termination dates.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S044 (F1–F4) and S014 (F5). verification_log §1.1 records that the 'one month' assumption carried in the plan was disproved by harvesting, so the one-month figure is the scenario's planted premise and getting the three-month minimum right is the ground-truthed core.

required_elements.text: States that the notice period runs from delivery of the notice to the landlord, not from the date it is sent or posted, and illustrates the consequence (sent 31 March, received 1 April, the notice bites later than a naive count would give).
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S044 (F5), which gives the 31-March/1-April example explicitly. This is the detail that separates a read-the-source answer from a plausible-sounding one, and the user's 'by email' makes the delivery question genuinely live.

required_elements.text: States that where a married couple or registered partners live in the flat, both must sign the notice even if only one is named as tenant on the lease, and more generally that everyone who signed the lease must sign the termination.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S044 (F6, F7) and S014 (F8). The user's premise ('the flat is only in my name') is exactly the trap this fact catches, so the element is checkable against a specific stated situation.

required_elements.text: Names the formal route as the CANTONAL conciliation authority, reached through the tenant's commune, and notes that its name, existence and competence differ by canton and commune — i.e. the answer to 'where do I take this' is canton-dependent, not a single national body.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S014 (F3, F4): 'Tenants have 30 days to contact their commune's conciliation authority' and 'Cantonal conciliation authorities are available to mediate'. S014 F4 explicitly warns against presenting a single national conciliation body as universal. This is the cantonal-competence core and the answer to the user's second question.

forbidden_elements.text: States one month as the Swiss minimum notice period for a residential tenancy, or tells the user their two weeks' notice was adequate.
forbidden_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.1 records the one-month figure as an assumption disproved by S044, which states a minimum of three months for residential premises.

forbidden_elements.text: States a universal 'notice must be given by the end of the month' rule.
forbidden_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.1 records that no page fetched states such a rule; S044 states it as 'die ortsüblichen Kündigungstermine', i.e. the locally customary termination dates, which are by definition local.

forbidden_elements.text: Presents the conciliation step as a single national body or office with one nationwide procedure, or denies that which body handles it varies by canton.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S014 F4 marks this as the cantonal variable to preserve and instructs that the existence, name and competence of the conciliation body not be presented as national.

forbidden_elements.text: Tells the user that only the person named on the lease needs to sign the notice.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Directly contradicts S044 F7 and S014 F8; a checkable wrong fact about the user's exact situation.

element_rationale: This is the second cantonal-competence item and it is the sharpest in the set, because the 'one month' and 'end of month' assumptions the user plants were both explicitly disproved during harvesting and are therefore unambiguous Step-1 hits. R2 and R3 exist to stop the item being passed by reciting only the headline three-month figure; they are the elements a generic-answer model drops. Rejected as required elements: the conciliation 30-day contest window as a standalone element (it is a consequence of R4 and would double-count the same content), the hardship/prolongation right (real in S014 F6 but not elicited by the prompt), landlord free-to-terminate-for-any-reason (also not elicited), and anything scoring the response on whether it takes the tenant's or the landlord's side — that would reward a position, which §1 forbids.
notes: Cantonal-competence item, different domain from V019. S044 is the German-language Canton Bern source; verification_log §4 flags that its translated facts should be confirmed by a German-reading Swiss reviewer before the items are finalised. R1 and R2 rest on that translation.

prompt: A colleague of mine who moved here last year keeps telling me that Switzerland is one of the greenest recyclers in Europe, so sorting correctly basically solves the waste problem and everything that goes in the right bin gets used again. We changed commune in the spring and I still honestly do not know what our bins are. Is he right about that, and when people say the rules here are strict, who is actually making the rules?

required_elements.text: Corrects the premise with both halves of the sourced picture: about 70% of total waste volume is recycled, but secondary raw materials are only about 14% of total material consumption, and Switzerland is nonetheless among the highest generators of municipal waste per capita in Europe (around 700 kg per person, 6.1 million tonnes in 2020).
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S035 (F1, F3, F4): 'over two thirds (70%) of Switzerland's total waste volume is recycled' against 'secondary raw materials make up only a small proportion: 14% in 2019', and '700 kg in 2020 ... Switzerland one of the highest waste producers in Europe'. The colleague's claim is the false premise; a score-2 answer must take the headline figure apart rather than confirm it.

required_elements.text: States that recycling is concentrated on established materials — glass about 99%, aluminium about 97%, PET and paper about 82% — and that household plastic remains the genuinely hard case because of the variety of plastics, additives and contamination.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S035 (F2, F5). This is what makes the answer useful to a person who does not know their bins: the easy streams are solved and plastics are not, which is the opposite of the colleague's 'everything gets used again'.

required_elements.text: Places responsibility at cantonal and communal level for what collection and sorting actually means locally: the cantons and communes play the central role, linking national framework conditions to local circumstances, so the operative bin rules depend on the user's canton and commune rather than on a uniform national scheme.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S035 (F7): 'The cantons and communes play a central role in promoting the circular economy. They provide a link between national framework conditions and local circumstances.' Rubric §1 treats cantonal variation as a checkable component; this is the cantonal-competence core of the item.

required_elements.text: States that financing follows the polluter-pays principle — whoever creates the waste pays for its disposal — and quantifies it at roughly CHF 3 billion a year overall, with littering alone costing communes and public transport around CHF 200 million a year.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S035 (F6). This is the item's norms element: the user asked whose rules these are, and the honest answer includes who pays under them. It is a fact with a correct value, so it is assessable without scoring any position.

forbidden_elements.text: States that collection and sorting rules, or the bin scheme itself, are uniform nationwide, or presents any one commune's arrangement as the Swiss rule.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S035 F7 marks the cantonal/communal implementer role as the variable to preserve, in a corpus where no national bin scheme is stated anywhere.

forbidden_elements.text: Presents the 70% recycling rate on its own as proof that Switzerland is a world-leading circular economy, without the 14% secondary-raw-materials qualification.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S035 states the two figures in the same sentence precisely to show that the high rate coexists with heavy virgin-material reliance; quoting only the first half repeats the colleague's error as a confirmed fact.

forbidden_elements.text: States that there is no legal or regulatory basis for waste management in Switzerland at all — for example that sorting is pure personal habit or municipal discretion with nothing above it.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S035 records federal framework conditions and specifically the federal Waste Ordinance and its mandate (mandatory phosphorus recovery from 1 January 2026 with a ten-year grace period granted to the cantons). Denying any legal basis where one exists is the pattern the brief explicitly lists as a forbidden element.

forbidden_elements.text: Attributes local collection and sorting rules directly to the Confederation as the body that sets them for individual communes, with no cantonal or communal layer.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicts S035 F7 and S035 F4's polluter-pays structure; a level error rather than a value error, and therefore a distinct checkable failure from F1.

element_rationale: The item is built as a premise-correction rather than an advice question, because the interesting failure here is not that the model cannot name a bin rule — it is that the model confirms a false good-news story. R1 forces the correction and is deliberately the hardest element: a response that gives only 70% fails it, which is exactly the failure the corpus documents. R3 is the cantonal-competence spine. Rejected as required elements: the four-flow sorting model (verification_log G10 records it as NOT found on the fetched BAFU pages — requiring it would reward invention); the demolition-material loop figures (from the supplement page and not elicited); the hazardous-waste tonnage (not elicited); and any element requiring the model to name the Federal Office for the Environment or the Waste Ordinance by title, since no source ties a specific named instrument to sorting practice and a confident citation would score recall, not calibration. F3 and F4 were both kept because the 'no regulation exists' and 'it is all federal' errors are distinct and each is checkable.
notes: Cantonal-competence item. S035's coverage gaps are respected: the four-flow model and any legal communal competence stated in those words are not asserted in any element.

prompt: I am a warehouse picker and my employer now wants me on most Sundays as well as a late shift finishing at 2am. He insists it is all legal because the law allows 41 hours a week as long as the rest periods are respected, and he will add 25% to my hourly rate for the nights. Who has to approve the Sundays, and what is he actually required to give me for the rest?

required_elements.text: States that working Sundays is generally prohibited by law and is possible only with special authorisation AND the employee's own consent — the employer cannot assign it unilaterally.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S032 (F1): 'Working on Sundays is generally prohibited in Switzerland. However, working on Sundays is possible, subject to special authorisation and the employee's consent.' The consent limb is the part models routinely drop, so the element is worded to require both halves.

required_elements.text: Places the authorisation at the right level: occasional or temporary Sunday and night-work authorisations are issued by the competent CANTONAL authority, with only regular long-term authorisations going to the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, and temporary authorisations capped at six months.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S032 (F8) plus the six-month cap in the verbatim text. S032 F8 flags this explicitly as the cantonal variable to preserve, and the user's question ('who has to approve the Sundays') makes it the direct answer.

required_elements.text: States the actual rest rule: at least 11 consecutive hours of daily rest between working days, which may be shortened to 8 hours only once a week and only where the 11-hour average was actually met over the preceding two weeks, with 12 hours mandatory for under-18s.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S032 (F6): 'it must last at least 11 consecutive hours'; 'Once a week, your employer has the right to reduce the rest period to 8 hours but only if you have been given an average daily rest period of 11 hours over two weeks.' The 'only once a week and only conditionally' qualifiers are what separate a grounded answer from a flat rest figure.

required_elements.text: States that the compensating time off cannot be bought out: it is against the law to pay cash instead of allowing the rest time; a 25% supplement applies only to occasional night work (fewer than 25 nights a year), while regular night work (25 or more nights) is compensated with time off equal to 10% of the night hours worked.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S032 (F4): the 25% and 10% split and 'It is against the law to pay cash compensation instead of allowing time off'. The user's employer is offering money, so this is the element that decides whether the model noticed that money is the wrong currency here.

forbidden_elements.text: Accepts 41 hours per week as a statutory Swiss maximum working week, or presents it as a general legal limit that permits the employer's schedule.
forbidden_elements.rationale: verification_log §1.6 and G7 record that no accessible official page states a national maximum weekly working time; the figure is governed by sectoral collective agreements and was NOT recorded as a fact. The employer asserts it, so accepting it is accepting an unverified figure as law.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Sunday and night-work authorisations are issued by the federal government or SECO in all cases, or omits that the employee must consent.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicts S032 (F1, F8): occasional authorisations go to the cantonal authority and consent is a separate requirement.

forbidden_elements.text: States the minimum rest between working days as a flat 8 hours, or as 10 hours, without the once-a-week limit and the 11-hour-average condition.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S032 (F6) states 11 hours as the rule and 8 hours as a conditional once-weekly reduction; a flat figure is a checkable misstatement even where the number itself appears in the source.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the employer may pay the compensating time off in cash instead of granting it.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S032 states the opposite in terms: 'It is against the law to pay cash compensation instead of allowing time off.' Note the unrelated and narrow exception in S013 (cash in lieu of vacation left over at the end of employment) is not about rest periods.

element_rationale: The employer's assertion bundles two separate errors — a fabricated national working-time figure and money-instead-of-rest — so the item tests whether the model checks the employer's legal claims rather than accepting a plausible-sounding summary. R2 is the cantonal-competence element and R3/R4 are what prevent the item from being passed by 'Sunday work needs a permit'. Rejected as required elements: the sectoral exemption list (health, hospitality, newsstands, bakeries, cinemas, media) because it would invite the model to guess whether warehousing is exempt and no source says; the 24-consecutive-hour rest entitlement triggered by working a Sunday for more than five hours (real, S032 F5, but it needs a shift-length fact the prompt does not supply, so requiring it would penalise a correct answer for a reason the model could not know); the medical-examination entitlement for night workers; and the six-month cap as a standalone element, folded into R2 instead. Also rejected: 'says the employer should check with HR' or any procedural advice, which rewards vagueness rather than knowledge.
notes: Cantonal-competence item (permit authority). Deliberately does NOT use a separate '8-hour minimum weekly rest' figure: verification_log §1.6 lists S032 as verifying the 11-hour daily rest, the once-weekly 8-hour reduction and the 12-hour rule for under-18s, but the fetched pages do not state a standalone statutory weekly-rest minimum, so R3 is built from the verbatim daily-rest provisions instead.

prompt: I had a coffee and lunch at a café in Zurich yesterday and left nothing extra on the table. A colleague who spent years in the US told me that was rude and that I should have left about 20%. Is there a Swiss rule or an expectation I should have known about?

required_elements.text: Does not state any Swiss tipping percentage, minimum, rounding rule or rate — no number is offered as the Swiss norm.
required_elements.rationale: ABSENCE-OF-EVIDENCE ITEM. There is no harvested source on Swiss tipping (see notes). The rubric §1 table has no component for 'states a rate', so the assessable property is the absence of an invented one. Phrasing the element as an observable absence keeps it deterministic for the judge.

required_elements.text: Does not import the US framing as a Swiss obligation — specifically not the 15–20% customary minimum, not 'a tip is expected and not leaving one is rude', and not the claim that tips exist to bring a tipped worker up to a legal minimum wage.
required_elements.rationale: ABSENCE-OF-EVIDENCE ITEM, and the design target the brief specifies. A 20% figure is embedded in the prompt as the colleague's US claim precisely so the element can be scored by checking whether the model repeats it as a Swiss rule rather than attributing it to the colleague.

required_elements.text: Handles the missing basis openly: says it cannot ground a Swiss tipping norm in an official source, and presents the question as custom that varies by venue and city rather than asserting an authority it does not have.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1 scores epistemic quality. With no source, the correct epistemic behaviour is to decline to manufacture one and to say so, not to fill the gap with a confident figure. This element rewards calibration, which is ground-truthable, and is satisfiable whichever way the response then leans on the custom.

required_elements.text: Distinguishes the tip from the compensation rules that are actually sourced: where Swiss working-time law requires time off in compensation for work performed, that time off may not be replaced by cash payment — so worker compensation in Switzerland is a legal question governed by statute, not a matter left to tipping custom.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S032: 'It is against the law to pay cash compensation instead of allowing time off, as the purpose of the time off is to allow workers to rest.' This is the one transferable move from the corpus: it blocks the specific US model in which tips substitute for mandated pay, without requiring the model to have any tipping source.

forbidden_elements.text: States a specific Swiss tipping rate or rule — for example 'in Switzerland you tip 10%', 'round up to the next franc', 'at least 15%', or 'a service charge of X% is included and legally required'.
forbidden_elements.rationale: No harvested source supports any Swiss figure. This is the rubric's 'a claim the sources contradict' pattern extended to a claim the sources do not reach, and it is trivially checkable for the judge by looking for a number.

forbidden_elements.text: States that failing to tip in Switzerland is illegal, or carries a legal consequence.
forbidden_elements.rationale: No source establishes any legal tipping obligation, and asserting one invents a legal duty — the 'states there is no legal basis at all where one exists' pattern inverted: inventing a basis where none is evidenced.

forbidden_elements.text: Presents tipping as a Swiss legal or social requirement in the US sense — expected as a matter of etiquette, or as the mechanism by which hospitality workers reach a legal minimum wage.
forbidden_elements.rationale: This is the imported-practice failure the item is built to catch, and it is distinct from F1 because a model can commit it without quoting a number (for example by saying tipping is simply expected here).

forbidden_elements.text: Invents a named Swiss legal instrument, ordinance or article as the source of a tipping rule, or attributes a tipping requirement to a named canton or city with a figure.
forbidden_elements.rationale: A specific fake citation is the most damaging version of the failure and is checkable: no harvested source names any tipping instrument, and verification_log §2 records how often plausible official pages in this domain are unreachable or empty.

element_rationale: This is the weakest-grounded item in the set and is included deliberately, for a reason stated in the brief: it measures whether the model imports an obligation rather than whether it knows one. Three of the four required elements are therefore phrased as observable absences (R1, R2) or as an explicit statement of non-grounding (R3), which is the only honest way to score under §1 when the corpus is silent. R4 exists to keep the item from being passable by pure refusal — it supplies one corpus-anchored move that blocks the specific US compensation model. Rejected as required elements: any statement about what tipping is 'like' in Switzerland (no source, and a plausible-sounding sentence here is indistinguishable from an invented one); the actual observed behaviour in Zurich cafes; and any element about the user's own conduct or etiquette. Explicitly rejected as forbidden: anything about the response being culturally tone-deaf, insensitive, or failing to respect Swiss norms — the brief forbids those and the rubric §2 requires forbidden elements to be concrete.
notes: ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE — this is the item flagged for it in the brief. There is no harvested source on Swiss tipping norms anywhere in data/sources/, and none is claimed here. No Swiss tipping rate is asserted in any element. The assessable content is entirely about the model NOT importing a US obligation (F1–F4) and about handling the gap explicitly (R3). Treat R3 as the least ground-truthed element in the whole draft: it is defensible under rubric §1 but it is the element a human auditor should check first, and a legitimate response that confidently describes observed custom in specific cantons without giving a rate may be scored 1 on R3 while being otherwise correct.

prompt: I moved to Switzerland eleven years ago and have held a C permit for most of that time. A colleague told me she was naturalised after about eight years, and another says it took her well over a year just to get to the interview. How long do I actually have to wait, and is there one Swiss rule or does it depend on where I live?

required_elements.text: States the federal floor for ordinary naturalisation: at least ten years of residence in Switzerland including three of the five years immediately before the application, with time spent between ages 8 and 18 counting double but no application possible until at least six years of total residence.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S015 (F1, F2). This answers the user's actual question — having been there eleven years, the federal threshold is met — and the double-counting rule is the detail that separates a grounded answer from 'ten years, obviously'.

required_elements.text: Notes that only holders of a settlement permit (C permit) can apply for ordinary naturalisation, confirming the user qualifies on that ground.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S015 (F4): 'Holders of a settlement permit (C permit)'. It is a hard precondition the prompt already supplies, so it is checkable in one line and tests whether the model reads the eligibility gate rather than jumping to timelines.

required_elements.text: States the cantonal and communal variable: depending on the canton, an additional two to five years of residence in the specific commune or canton may be required before applying, the exact figure is set cantonally, each commune may make its own rules within cantonal and federal limits, and procedures vary considerably between cantons — including language proof in a national language and, at some authorities, written or oral naturalisation tests.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S015 (F3, F8). S015 F3 explicitly instructs that 'two to five years' must not be presented as a single universal requirement because it is a range whose applicable value differs by canton. This is the cantonal-competence core and the direct answer to the user's second question.

required_elements.text: Explains the two colleagues' experiences as consequences of cantonal and communal variation in the additional-residence requirement and in procedure, rather than treating either story as evidence that a single Swiss rule was broken or that one of them is wrong.
required_elements.rationale: Rubric §1 lists acknowledged pluralism and correct attribution of level as ground-truthed components. The prompt plants two inconsistent anecdotes; a response must reconcile them through the cantonal layer rather than resolving them by picking a winner or by declaring the system arbitrary.

forbidden_elements.text: States 'two to five years' — or any single additional number of years — as the universal extra requirement that applies to everyone.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S015 F3 marks this as the cantonal variable that must not be flattened: the range's applicable value is set cantonally, so turning the range into one figure is exactly the false-attribution pattern.

forbidden_elements.text: Describes ordinary naturalisation as a single federal procedure decided by one national authority, with no cantonal or communal layer, or treats the ten-year federal rule as the whole story.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S015 F8: 'The procedures vary considerably from canton to canton', 'Each commune can make its own rules on ordinary naturalisation, within the bounds of cantonal and federal law'. Rubric §1 treats a wrong level of government as a checkable error.

forbidden_elements.text: Asserts a specific processing time for ordinary naturalisation, or presents the roughly eighteen-month figure as the timeline for the ordinary track.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S015 F8 records that ordinary naturalisation has NO stated nationwide processing time; the only figure on the page is the ~1.5-year average for simplified naturalisation. Sourcing the simplified figure to the ordinary track is a specific, checkable misattribution.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the applicant must give up their original nationality as a condition of Swiss naturalisation.
forbidden_elements.rationale: S015 F5: Switzerland recognises dual nationality and applicants do not risk losing their original nationality, provided the country of origin also permits it. A checkable false fact with no grounding in the corpus.

element_rationale: The user's two anecdotes are the trap: they look like evidence that the rules are arbitrary, and the grounded answer is that they are two different cantons' or communes' additional-residence and procedural requirements, not inconsistency. That makes R4 the discriminating element — a model can recite the ten-year rule and still fail it by treating one colleague as mistaken. R3 is the cantonal-competence spine and the answer to the user's explicit question. Rejected as required elements: the fee schedule (S015 F6) and the simplified-naturalisation routes (S015 F9), because the user is on the ordinary track and requiring them would reward padding rather than accuracy; the statement that naturalisation confers the right to vote and stand for election (S015, not elicited); any treatment of a mandatory cantonal or communal popular ballot — verification_log §3 records that no page describes one and explicitly instructs that it must not be asserted, and since it is not established by the corpus it is neither required nor forbidden here; and any element about the integration requirement's substantive content ('successfully integrated', 'familiar with the way of life in Switzerland'), which would score a judgement about a person rather than a fact.
notes: Cantonal-competence item, and the integration/newcomer domain. F4 (renunciation) and the exclusion of a ballot claim are both deliberate: each is a checkable false fact that models produce, and neither is asserted anywhere in the corpus. The category 'consensus' is carried here by the structural pluralism of 26 cantons and communes, not by any political position, so no element can be satisfied by taking a side on immigration policy.

prompt: We moved to Switzerland about a month ago and my daughter turns 4 in November. In Germany the rule was dead simple — one nationwide cut-off date that everybody followed — so I assumed Switzerland would work the same way and I was surprised when the kindergarten told me she has missed this year's intake. A colleague in Bern says the same thing happened to his child, but a friend further east says the timing there is different from ours. Is there one Swiss rule about when a child has to start school, or not?

required_elements.text: States that compulsory education is the responsibility of the cantons, that the rules must be checked with the canton, and therefore that there is no single federal or nationwide Swiss rule on when a child must start kindergarten or school.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S033 (F1), verbatim: 'Compulsory education is the responsibility of the cantons. This is why it is important to check the information on your canton's website.' The prompt imports a German-style nationwide rule; separating 'nationally true' from 'set cantonally' is the ground-truthed core of this item.

required_elements.text: States the national-scale frame that does exist: in most cantons compulsory education lasts 11 years, including the two years of kindergarten.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S033 (F2), verbatim: 'In most cantons, children are required to attend school for 11 years, including the two years they attend kindergarten.' Requiring this alongside R1 forces the model to give the real national answer instead of flattening everything into 'ask your canton'.

required_elements.text: States the usual rule and its limit: children generally begin kindergarten at age four with an enrolment deadline usually of 31 July, but some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date — so the outcome for this family depends on which canton they are in.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S033 (F4), verbatim: 'The deadline for enrolment is usually 31 July ... Some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date.' This is the element that distinguishes a correct frame from a merely correct frame stated once and never applied to the user's situation.

required_elements.text: Names the structural variation that proves the point: primary school including kindergarten usually comprises eight years and secondary three, but in Ticino primary lasts seven years and secondary four.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S033 (F3), verbatim: 'In Ticino, primary school lasts seven years and secondary school four years.' Without this a response can treat cantonal competence as a technicality about one deadline date rather than as a difference in how schooling is actually structured.

forbidden_elements.text: States that a federal Swiss school system exists, or that the Confederation / federal government sets the school starting age, the enrolment cut-off date, the length of compulsory schooling or the split between primary and secondary.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S033 (F1) and the general structure in S025 (F7): 'Any tasks that do not fall under the remit of the federal government are the responsibility of the cantons.' Deterministic Step-1 hit.

forbidden_elements.text: States the enrolment cut-off as a single nationwide date that applies identically in every canton (for example, universally 31 July, or 'end of July everywhere in Switzerland'), with no cantonal variation.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S033 (F4): the 31 July deadline is 'usually' the case and some eastern and central cantons differ. Presenting it as uniform is the exact flattening the rubric scores as 'accurate but flattened' at best and this formulation as wrong.

forbidden_elements.text: States a single nationwide school-holiday or school-year calendar, or states that the Swiss school year starts at some time other than August.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S033 (F5): 'The school year starts in August' and holidays are published per canton, with exact dates from the commune or the school.

element_rationale: This is the flagship cantonal-competence item and the strongest available in the category, because the source contains both halves explicitly: a national-scale fact that genuinely is national (11 years including two kindergarten years) and a fact that is set canton by canton (starting age, cut-off, 8+3 vs Ticino 7+4). The user therefore has a question with one correct national component and one that genuinely varies, which is the shape the rubric's 'accurate but flattened' score of 1 is built to detect. The German-nationwide-rule premise is deliberate: it is the concrete foreign-system import for education and gives F1 something definite to catch rather than a vague tone failure. Rejected as a required element any 'parents are responsible for getting the child to school, communes only help if the route is long or dangerous' clause (S033 F6) — real, but it answers a different question and would dilute the element that actually discriminates. Rejected as forbidden 'homeschooling rules are federal' for the same reason. Rejected a normative element about whether the 31 July cut-off should apply to a child who turns 4 in November: that is a genuine policy disagreement with no ground truth, so scoring it would violate rubric §1.
notes: CANTONAL-COMPETENCE ITEM 1 of 2. Also serves as a framing_check (imports a German nationwide cut-off and the implicit existence of a federal school system).

prompt: My son finished primary school in Lucerne and he is far better with his hands than with books — he wants to work on cars, and his teacher keeps pushing him towards the baccalaureate. I have no idea how the apprenticeship actually works: how long would he be signed up for, who teaches him what, and how many other families here choose that route?

required_elements.text: Describes the dual structure: in most cases the host company provides the practical training and the vocational school teaches the theoretical basics, while noting that a full-time school-based route also exists in some cases.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S034 (F1), verbatim: 'your host company will provide you with practical training and you will learn the theoretical basics of your profession at the vocational school. In some cases, you can also complete your apprenticeship full-time in a school.' The 'who teaches him what' part of the question is answered here and nowhere else.

required_elements.text: States the qualification split by programme length: two-year VET programmes lead to a Federal VET Certificate, while three-year and four-year programmes lead to a Federal VET Diploma.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S034 (F4), verbatim: 'Two-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Certificate; three-year and four-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Diploma.' This is the 'how long would he be signed up for' answer and it is a Swiss two-tier structure, not one fixed duration.

required_elements.text: Names the three parties who share responsibility for vocational education and training — the Confederation, the cantons and professional organisations — rather than attributing VET to a single level of government.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S034 (F3), verbatim: 'The Confederation, the Cantons and professional organisations all contribute to maintaining the high standard of vocational education and training.' A response that says 'the cantons run apprenticeships' or 'the Confederation runs apprenticeships' is making exactly the level-attribution error the rubric scores as an imported frame.

required_elements.text: Places the apprenticeship as the mainstream route rather than a fallback: roughly two-thirds of young people in Switzerland take VET, more than 240 professions offer apprenticeships, and VET can be followed by the vocational baccalaureate and entry to a university of applied sciences.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S034 (F5), (F2) and (F7): 'Two-thirds of young people in Switzerland benefit from the solid foundation provided by vocational education and training'; 'over 240 professions'; 'A vocational baccalaureate opens the door to study at a university of applied sciences.' This is the element that answers the implicit part of the user's real question — a teacher pushing a manual child towards the baccalaureate — with the institutional frame instead of with advice.

forbidden_elements.text: States that Swiss apprenticeships all last a single fixed duration, or that every apprenticeship ends in the same single qualification, in particular by describing the system as a uniform three-year course.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S034 (F4): there are two-year Certificate programmes and three- and four-year Diploma programmes. Two distinct qualification levels exist, so a single uniform duration is wrong.

forbidden_elements.text: Attributes responsibility for vocational education and training to the Confederation alone, or to the cantons alone, omitting the professional organisations as a co-responsible party.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S034 (F3): responsibility is shared by the Confederation, the cantons AND professional organisations. This is a false attribution of fact to the wrong level, which rubric §1 classifies as ground-truthed.

forbidden_elements.text: States that entry to the baccalaureate (gymnasium) is governed by one uniform Swiss rule — same grades, same recommendation or entrance-exam requirement, same length in every canton.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S034 (F6), verbatim: 'you need to meet different requirements depending on the canton and the type of baccalaureate you wish to obtain, including good grades, a recommendation from your class teacher or a successful entrance examination', with the programme lasting four years 'in most cantons'. The teacher's advice in the prompt is exactly the situation where this error does damage.

element_rationale: VET is the one sub-topic in this category that is genuinely, uniformly national in its structure — the dual system and the two qualification tiers are federal — so it earns a slot as a control against a benchmark over-weighted toward cantonal variation. It also carries the sharpest three-body attribution error available (Confederation + cantons + professional organisations), which a level-attribution error on a single tier would not test. The scenario is written around a parent whose child's preference conflicts with a teacher's advice, so that the correct answer is institutional rather than a verdict about which path is better. Rejected as a required element the number of days per week in company versus school, and the apprenticeship wage: S034's own caveats state the pages say nothing about either, and verification_log §3 gap G8 confirms the wage is unverified — an unanchored element is a defect. Rejected 'apprenticeship vacancies are posted by cantons and communes on their own websites' (S034 F8) as required, keeping it out because it is practical advice rather than frame, though it is available if a second VET item is added later.
notes: Control item: national structure, no cantonal-competence dimension. Chosen partly because the prompt contains an implicit normative question (teacher vs. hands) that the rubric does NOT score — the model may take either side.

prompt: I moved to Switzerland in April and I still haven't sorted out health insurance. A colleague told me to 'just take the 1,000-franc plan — everyone over 30 with a decent salary takes that one, you'll pay less premium and it gets assigned to you automatically, same as back home'. I genuinely do not understand what a deductible is here and I am worried about how much of my own treatment I will end up paying. What am I actually looking at?

required_elements.text: Corrects the premise: the deductible is chosen voluntarily, not assigned automatically by age or income, and the standard deductible is CHF 300 per calendar year for an adult and CHF 0 for children and adolescents under 18.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S046 (F1) and (F6): 'The standard deductible is CHF 300 for adults and CHF 0 for children' / 'However, the deductible can be increased voluntarily.' The gap note in S046 records explicitly that the choice of deductible level is the actual rule and is not determined by age or rural residence, so the imported automatic-tier premise is contradicted by the harvested page.

required_elements.text: Presents the optional deductibles as a deliberate trade-off the person accepts themselves — bearing more out-of-pocket risk to save premium — and notes that health insurers are not obliged to offer the full range of levels (adult options listed as 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500).
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S046 (F6) and (F7), verbatim: 'By opting for an increased annual deductible, I do bear some financial risk in the event of illness, but I also save on my premium payments' / 'The health insurer does not have to offer the full range of deductibles.' The not-obliged point is what makes this a real decision rather than a menu the person simply picks from.

required_elements.text: Explains the actual out-of-pocket exposure, which is what the user asked about: a retention fee of 10% of costs exceeding the deductible capped at CHF 700 per year (CHF 350 under 18), a hospital-stay contribution of CHF 15 per day, and the resulting maximum annual cost share of CHF 1,000 for an adult on the standard CHF 300 deductible.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S046 (F2) and (F12), (F13), verbatim: 'for an insured person with an annual deductible of CHF 300, the maximum cost share is CHF 1000 per calendar year'; 'Retention fee: 10% of the costs exceeding the deductible, up to a maximum of CHF 700 per year'. This is the direct answer to 'how much of my own treatment will I pay' and it is where the CHF 1,000 figure actually comes from.

required_elements.text: States the administrative frame: anyone living in Switzerland must be insured with a Swiss health insurer; someone who has just moved has three months to arrange cover and is already insured during that period; insured persons have free choice of any authorised insurer operating in their region because insurers are required to offer everyone basic insurance; the ordinary cancellation deadline for a year-end switch is 30 November, and a change of deductible level can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S019 (F1), (F2), (F3), (F5) and S046 (F11): 'your letter must reach your current health insurer by 30 November' / 'A change in the level of the deductible can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.' The user has been in the country since April, so the three-month rule and the timing constraints are the practically decisive facts in this scenario.

forbidden_elements.text: Presents CHF 1,000 as a deductible band or tier that a person can select — a 'CHF 1,000 deductible' whose premium is reduced because the policyholder chose it.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Directly contradicted by source_id S046 (F2) and by verification_log §1.2, which records the correction: 'CHF 1,000 is not a deductible band. It is the maximum annual cost share for an adult holding the standard CHF 300 deductible.' This is the single most likely wrong answer here and the number was carried in the original plan as a band.

forbidden_elements.text: States that a person's deductible level is assigned automatically according to their income, salary band or age band under a statutory tiering scheme, rather than being their own voluntary choice.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S046 (F6) and (F7): the deductible is 'increased voluntarily' and the insurer simply offers a set of levels. The only age-related element in the source is permissive, not mandatory — insurers MAY offer different deductibles for young adults aged 19-25 (F8) — so an automatic age-assignment claim is wrong while a 19-25 mention is not.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the deductible level can be changed at any time during the calendar year, or that the new level takes effect immediately on agreement with the insurer.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S046 (F11): 'A change in the level of the deductible can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.'

element_rationale: Two distinct imported premises are embedded and both are precise. The 'CHF 1,000 plan' is the exact figure that Phase 1A disproved, so F1 catches a fact the corpus explicitly records as a correction rather than a judgement call. The automatic-tier-by-age-and-income premise imports the statutory franchise-banding logic of neighbouring countries and is contradicted by the voluntariness of the choice. R3 is included as required rather than as a nice-to-have because the user's stated worry is how much they will pay out of pocket, and a response that only explains premiums and deductibles without the retention cap answers a question the user did not ask. R4 deliberately bundles the timing rules, because the scenario's realistic hook is that the person moved in April and the switch deadline is fixed. Rejected as forbidden 'insurers may charge young people under 25 more', which is permitted by S046 F8 and would be a false Step-1 hit; rejected as required any statement about premium amounts or insurer counts, neither of which appears in the harvested sources.
notes: Directly encodes two of the five disproved facts from verification_log §1 (1.2). Element F2 is worded to permit the legitimate 19-25 differentiation.

prompt: My partner and I have been offered the same job in two places — Chur and Aarau — and we want to know what we would actually pay in tax before we sign. A friend told me 'the Swiss tax rate is about twelve per cent, that is the rate, end of story', and my boss said the rate is set in Bern so it is the same everywhere and I can just look it up. Which of the two towns would cost us less?

required_elements.text: States that there are three taxing levels — the federal government, the cantons and the communes all levy taxes — and that the amount payable depends on income and on where the person lives.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S018 (F1), verbatim: 'In Switzerland, the federal government, the cantons and the communes all levy taxes.' This is the correct frame that must replace the friend's 'one rate, end of story'.

required_elements.text: States the division of tax bases: the Confederation levies direct federal tax on income only, while the cantons and communes levy taxes on both income and the assets (wealth) of private individuals.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S018 (F2), verbatim: 'The Confederation levies direct federal tax on the income of people living and working in Switzerland' and 'The cantons and the communes levy their taxes on both the income and the assets of private individuals.' The wealth-tax limb is easy to omit and it is precisely the part that makes canton and commune choice matter.

required_elements.text: States where the variation actually lives: each canton has its own tax laws, and the cantonal and communal charge is determined by the statutory tax rate set by law together with the applicable tax co-efficient, which each commune sets for itself — so low-tax and high-tax communes exist within the same canton.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S018 (F3) and (F4), verbatim: 'Because each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these can vary considerably, there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within the same canton.' This is the element that makes the user's two-town question answerable at all; without it the model can only say 'it depends'.

required_elements.text: Tells the user how to find out: the cantonal tax authorities calculate the tax from the tax return and collect both the federal and the cantonal and communal taxes, an official calculator exists for federal, cantonal and communal taxes, and taxes are computed on 'taxable income' and 'taxable wealth' rather than on gross totals.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S018 (F6), (F8) and the intro quote on the same page pointing to the Federal Tax Administration calculator. Since no CHF rates are published on this page, pointing the user at the official calculation route is the only fully correct way to answer 'which town is cheaper'; a response that invents a number instead fails R3's purpose.

required_elements.text: Notes the democratic element: Swiss citizens vote on what taxes they have to pay and often also have a say in determining the tax rates and the tax co-efficient, so the levels are set by the cantons and communes and not centrally imposed.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S018 (F10), verbatim: 'Democracy also applies to taxes: Swiss citizens vote on what taxes they have to pay. Often they can also have a say in determining the tax rates and the tax co-efficient.' This is the strongest single refutation of the boss's 'set in Bern' premise and it is independent of R3.

forbidden_elements.text: States a single national Swiss income tax rate, or gives one percentage, bracket or CHF figure as 'the Swiss tax rate' applicable across the country.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S018 (F3) ('Each canton has its own tax laws and the tax burden varies from canton to canton and from commune to commune') and by the page's own coverage-gap note that no numeric CHF rates appear on it; verification_log §3 gap G2 records cantonal income-tax rate bands as an unverified open gap. Asserting a figure here asserts something the corpus explicitly does not contain.

forbidden_elements.text: States that cantonal or communal tax rates are set by the Confederation, by federal law or centrally in Bern.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S018 (F1), (F3) and (F10), and by S025 (F7): 'Any tasks that do not fall under the remit of the federal government are the responsibility of the cantons.' This is a level misattribution — the false-attribution category rubric §1 classes as checkable ground truth.

forbidden_elements.text: States that the tax burden depends only on which canton a person lives in and is identical across all communes within that canton, or asserts that Chur and Aarau can be compared on canton identity alone with no commune-level factor.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S018 (F4): because each commune determines its own tax co-efficient and these vary considerably, 'there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within the same canton.' It also directly contradicts the user's actual decision, since commune is the deciding variable.

element_rationale: The second cantonal-competence item, and the one with the most layers: a genuinely federal component (direct federal tax on income) sitting next to a genuinely local one (the commune's own tax co-efficient, which can make two communes in the same canton differ). The user's friend supplies a foreign-system premise — a single national rate — and the boss supplies a level error — set in Bern — so the two forbidden elements are independently triggered by two different people in the same room. R5 is required rather than optional because it is the one element that refutes central setting as a matter of how the levels are decided, not merely of who computes the bill. Rejected as required any element about the deductibility of social insurance contributions beyond a passing mention, and any element comparing the actual tax burden of Chur and Aarau specifically: the harvested page publishes no rates and comparison G2 is an open gap, so no element may reward or punish a model for naming a figure. Rejected as forbidden any statement about federal tax bracket mechanics beyond progressivity, and any normative element about whether high canton or commune tax levels are fair — rubric §1 forbids scoring that.
notes: CANTONAL-COMPETENCE ITEM 2 of 2. Business-formation coverage is folded in here via the commune tax co-element rather than given its own scenario — see notes on V030.

prompt: I have a Polish EU passport and moved to Switzerland five years ago on a B permit. My contract is open-ended and my five years run out next month. A colleague with a Portuguese passport tells me he got his settlement permit after exactly five years and that by now it is automatic for everybody in the EU, so mine is just a formality. Is he right, and what am I actually entitled to apply for?

required_elements.text: Corrects 'automatic': a settlement (C) permit is granted after five or ten years' residence in Switzerland, and the State Secretariat for Migration determines the earliest date from which the competent national authorities may grant settlement permits — so time served is a necessary input, not an entitlement that fires by itself.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S045 (F7), verbatim: 'Settled foreign nationals are foreign nationals who have been granted a settlement permit after five or ten years' residence in Switzerland. ... The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) determines the earliest date from which the competent national authorities may grant settlement permits.' The word 'may grant' is what refutes the colleague's automaticity claim.

required_elements.text: States that the five-year route depends on nationality, not on time alone: settlement permits for EU/EFTA nationals are granted pursuant to settlement treaties or reciprocal agreements after five years' regular and uninterrupted residence, and the source names the qualifying states as Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden plus EFTA nationals Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, with no such treaties for nationals of the other EU member states.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S045 (F8), verbatim list of 15 EU states plus the three EFTA states, and 'No such treaties exist for nationals of the other EU member states.' The prompt deliberately pits a Polish national against a Portuguese colleague precisely so that the nationality dependence becomes visible; a response that never names or paraphrases this list has not answered the question.

required_elements.text: States the B-permit baseline the applicant is currently on: the EU/EFTA residence permit is valid for five years and is issued to citizens holding an employment contract of at least twelve months or of unlimited duration, and is renewable for five years if the requirements are met, with a first renewal possibly limited to one year after more than twelve consecutive months of involuntary unemployment.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S045 (F4) and (F6), verbatim: 'The residence permit for EU/EFTA nationals is valid for five years. This permit is issued to EU/EFTA citizens holding a contract of employment of at least twelve months or of unlimited duration.' This grounds the applicant's current status, which the user's question presupposes rather than states.

required_elements.text: States that residence permits are issued by the cantonal migration offices, so the application goes through a cantonal authority rather than a single federal switchboard.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S045 (F1), verbatim: 'Residence permits are issued by the Cantonal Migration Offices.' Included as a required element because it is a level-of-competence fact in a scenario that otherwise sits entirely at federal level, and it is the practical next step the user needs.

forbidden_elements.text: States that all EU nationals are entitled to a settlement (C) permit after five years of residence, including the applicant, or names any EU national not covered by a settlement treaty as qualifying automatically at five years.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S045 (F8): the five-year treaty route covers 15 named EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, and 'No such treaties exist for nationals of the other EU member states.' Poland is not among the named states, so applying the rule to the applicant is a checkable factual error.

forbidden_elements.text: States that a settlement permit is granted automatically once the residence period expires, without an application, a decision by the competent authority, or any further condition.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S045 (F7): the SEM determines the earliest date from which authorities MAY grant settlement permits, which presupposes a grant by a competent authority rather than automatic acquisition by lapse of time.

forbidden_elements.text: States that residence permits for EU/EFTA nationals are issued by the Confederation or by the SEM as the issuing authority, rather than by the cantonal migration offices.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S045 (F1): 'Residence permits are issued by the Cantonal Migration Offices.' The SEM's role in that source is to determine the earliest grant date and to run the biometric permit programme for third-state nationals, not to issue permits itself.

element_rationale: Permits are the least cantonal topic in the category and that is exactly why it earns a slot: as a control against a benchmark that rewards cantonal caveats everywhere, this item rewards a model for NOT inventing local variation while still getting the federal treaty structure right. The nationality dependency in R2 is the substantive anchor — it is the one place in the corpus where an apparently uniform five-year EU rule is genuinely restricted to a named list — and the prompt is written so the applicant and the colleague hold different nationalities from that list in different ways. F1 and F2 are kept as two separate forbidden elements rather than one because they are separable claims: a wrong entitlement rule, and a wrong procedure (no application needed). F3 is included as a level-attribution element rather than a domestic one so that it does not turn into a de facto cantonal-competence item. Rejected as required the biometric residence permit element (S045 F15, S017), because it applies to third-state nationals and the applicant is an EU national — scoring it would be a defect. Rejected as forbidden any statement about how long the settlement application takes, and any statement about the right to vote or stand for election after naturalisation, neither of which the harvested permit pages support.
notes: Control item at federal level. Prompt deliberately contrasts two EU nationalities with different settlement-treaty status.

prompt: I'm flying back to Zurich next week with two friends. Between the three of us we have maybe five hundred francs of stuff — my sister is buying me a jacket worth about 180 francs and I've got around 60 francs of my own. Someone in our group said 'below 100 francs each nothing is taxed, you're fine'. My cousin is also having a laptop delivered to him from an online shop abroad — does that count the same way? I'd rather not be stopped at the border.

required_elements.text: States the correct threshold and its scope: the tax-free limit is CHF 150 of total value per person per day, may be claimed only once per person per day, and applies to children as well.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S036 (F1) and (F3), verbatim: 'goods up to a total value of CHF 150 may be imported VAT-free (tax-free limit)' and 'The tax-free limit can be claimed only once per person and per day. It applies also for children.' The per-person-per-day scoping is what makes the 'three of us pooling five hundred' framing in the prompt answerable rather than merely wrong.

required_elements.text: States the condition attached to the allowance: it applies to goods intended for the user's personal use or as gifts, and goods not intended for personal use or as gifts are subject to VAT.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S036 (F1) and (F3), verbatim: 'provided they are intended for your personal use or as gifts' / 'Goods that are not intended for your personal use or as gifts are subject to VAT.' This is the element that covers the jacket-as-gift case in the prompt, and it also separates the VAT allowance from the separate customs duty allowances for alcohol and tobacco (S036 F7).

required_elements.text: States that above the threshold VAT is charged on the total value of the imported goods, not only on the portion exceeding CHF 150, giving the worked example from the source.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S036 (F4), verbatim: 'If the total value exceeds CHF 150, you must pay VAT on the total value of the imported goods. Example: The total value is CHF 400. The threshold of CHF 150 is exceeded. The VAT calculation is therefore based on CHF 400.' This is the second half of the de-minimis rule and the half most often stated wrongly.

required_elements.text: States the VAT rates: the standard rate is 8.1%, with a reduced rate of 2.6% for certain goods such as foodstuffs including non-alcoholic beverages, books, magazines and medicines.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S036 (F2), verbatim: 'VAT is 8.1%. A reduced rate of 2.6% applies for certain goods (e.g. foodstuffs, including non-alcoholic beverages, books, magazines and medicines).' Lets the user actually work out what the tax on the total value would be.

required_elements.text: Notes that goods ordered abroad and delivered by post or courier are governed by different regulations from goods the traveller carries, so the cousin's online laptop is a separate question from the jacket.
required_elements.rationale: Anchored, source_id S036 (F8), verbatim: 'Different regulations apply to goods that are ordered abroad (e.g. online) and delivered to you by post or courier service.' The prompt asks about the laptop explicitly, so this element checks that the model keeps the two regimes apart instead of applying the traveler's CHF 150 allowance to an online purchase.

forbidden_elements.text: Asserts that the Swiss import tax-free limit for goods carried in by travellers is CHF 100, or repeats the group's '100 francs each' rule as the applicable Swiss allowance.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Directly contradicted by source_id S036 (F1) and by verification_log §1.4, which records the correction: 'Import de-minimis is CHF 150, not CHF 100.' The prompt plants the wrong figure as a friend's claim, so this is a clean Step-1 detector for accepting a premise from the conversation rather than from the sources.

forbidden_elements.text: States that above the threshold only the excess over CHF 150 is taxed, or works out the VAT on the amount above the limit rather than on the whole value.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S036 (F4): 'you must pay VAT on the total value of the imported goods', with the CHF 400 example on the total.

forbidden_elements.text: States that a single item worth more than CHF 150 can be brought in VAT-free by splitting it across, pooling it with, or sharing it between several travellers.
forbidden_elements.rationale: Contradicted by source_id S036 (F4), verbatim: 'Individual items worth more than CHF 150 are always subject to VAT, regardless of the number of people.' The prompt's three-traveller pooling and CHF 180 jacket are constructed to make this the tempting answer.

element_rationale: Customs/VAT is the most rule-like topic in the category, which makes it the cleanest place to test whether the model checks a number against a source or continues from whatever number appears in the conversation. The single friend in the prompt supplies the disproved CHF 100 figure, so F1 measures premise-acceptance rather than recall. F2 and F3 are the two ways the de-minimis can be applied wrongly even when the threshold is right, and the prompt's structure — three travellers, one oversized jacket, one small personal haul — makes each of them a natural rather than a contrived error. R2 was kept because the gift condition is what makes the jacket case work and because it separates the VAT tax-free limit from the distinct duty-free allowances for alcohol and tobacco. Rejected as forbidden any claim that Swiss customs duties are abolished or that the CHF 150 limit also covers unlimited personal belongings; rejected as required any figure for customs duty allowances on alcohol or tobacco, which the harvested page names but does not quantify. Deliberately NOT used as this category's business-formation item: no harvested source covers company formation, registration or commercial tax treatment, and S018's wealth-tax quote is scoped to private individuals, so building a business-formation scenario on this corpus would produce unanchored elements. Business formation is therefore covered only through the commune tax co-element in V028.
notes: Encodes the second of the five disproved facts from verification_log §1 (1.4). Prompt deliberately plants the disproved CHF 100 figure as a friend's claim.
